topics.topic: Atomic ordering of session validity, last-request refresh, and expiry
questions: How is an arriving request's validity check and last-request update ordered atomically against the expiry pass's decision, and does the request take the session lock for that operation?
When and under what lock is `last_request` updated, especially if a request arrives before the idle limit but waits for the import or session lock until after it?
How is `last_request` updated atomically against the expiry pass and concurrent arrivals?

quotes:
An owner
   request is any request to the owner interface that
   carries the valid session, whatever its answer; its arrival restarts the 30
   minutes — of concurrent requests the latest arrival counts; before the
   first request it runs from the sign-in.

Validity is
   checked when a request arrives (A04 rule 6, stage 1); a request that
   passes it completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs, and
   a restart that interrupts it leaves nothing of it (A04 rule 4).
judgement.why: P6 already judged how arrival and idle renewal are ordered against expiry sweeps on these unchanged passages.

precedent.topic: How request arrival is recorded and ordered against session expiry sweeps
quotes:

   passes it completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs, and
   a restart that interrupts it leaves nothing of it (A04 rule 4).
precedent.why: Validity and idle renewal are explicitly decided at request arrival, so a request arriving before the limit remains admitted even if a sweep later obtains the lock.

topics.topic: Cleanup-pass first-run, cadence, delay, overlap, and catch-up rules
questions: When is the first pass, and after a delayed pass is the next pass tied to the original 60-second schedule or to completion of the delayed pass?
Does the first pass occur at process start or 60 seconds later, and what happens to missed or overlapping ticks when a pass lasts more than 60 seconds or the clock changes?
What are the exact first-run, delay, overlap and catch-up rules for the 60-second cleanup pass?

quotes:
Registry
   ends it — and drops its pending confirmation and its uploaded file with it
   (M11) — at a pass over the sessions it makes every 60 seconds from the
   start; the pass alone ends sessions by their limits, taking the import
   lock and then each session's lock (A16 rule 2) and deciding under them.

A session that has reached a limit serves no request from that
   moment: a request carrying it is refused at the session check.
judgement.why: The limits themselves determine request refusal exactly, so the first tick, delayed-tick policy and overlap handling affect only internal reclamation of already inaccessible session state.

topics.topic: Complete configuration variable names, syntax, and validity rules
questions: What exact syntax and validity checks make the store location, backup location, owner credential, backup key and service tokens well formed beyond the separately stated length, distinctness and path checks?
What are the exact environment-variable names and the accepted syntax and encoding of each path and secret value?
What are the complete variable names and exact well-formedness rules for the store path, backup path, backup key, owner credential and four service tokens?

quotes:
The configuration is the set of environment variables whose names begin
   with `REGISTRY_`, set as R0-23 says; no other variable is read or
   checked.
judgement.why: Exact environment-variable names, textual encodings and value syntaxes are configuration field names and contract representations owned by State 6.

topics.topic: Owner-only mode selection and deterministic configuration-check precedence
questions: At what point is all-four versus owner-only mode selected, and which deterministic failure is reported when only some service-token variables are present or one is malformed?
At what point is the all-four-or-none alternative decided, and which missing token is reported first when only some tokens are present?
How does the presence check distinguish a valid owner-only configuration from an invalid configuration missing all four tokens?
What is the total order of all individual configuration checks, including the four tokens and the owner-only alternative, so the first diagnostic is deterministic?

quotes:
It holds exactly these items and no other: the store's
   location; the backup location and the backup key (A18); the owner
   credential; one service token for each service of A09 — PresuPro, Client
   Portal, Cabinet, Cabinet Kernel (R0-20, R0-23) — or, for an owner-only
   start, none of the four: Registry then serves the owner interface alone
   and refuses every service call (A18 rule 9).

The checks run in one
   order and the first that fails stops the start: no unknown item, taken in
   the order of their names by Unicode code point; every item of rule 1 present; each well formed; each secret's length (rule 3);
   their distinctness (rule 4); the store and backup location apart (rule
   5); the backup location writable, by a probe file under the temporary
   prefix (A18 rule 5); the store opening, or made new (rule 5). Within one
   check, items go in the order rule 1 lists them.

A configuration with some service tokens but without Client Portal's
   stops the start and names the missing item; one with none of the four is
   an owner-only start.
judgement.divergence: With a partial token set containing several simultaneous defects, one implementation selects the all-token mode and reports the first missing token in one service order, while another validates a present malformed token or chooses another missing token first; the owner sees a different startup diagnostic and correction sequence.
judgement.why: The valid all-or-none alternatives are answered, but the individual token order and precedence between selecting the alternative, presence checks and well-formedness checks are not.

topics.topic: Reservation and ordering of admitted requests against expiry, sign-out, and imports
questions: If an upload, mapping, confirmation or sign-out passes the session check but waits for the import/session locks, may the expiry pass end and remove that session before the admitted request acquires the locks, and if so how can that request still complete without recreating state in an ended session?

After an owner request has passed the session check but before it acquires the import lock, what event is its semantic ordering point against an accepted import or session expiry: session-check time, import-lock acquisition, session-lock acquisition, or transaction commit?
What makes admission atomic with the expiry pass or sign-out, so an admitted request cannot later find that its session and pending state were removed before it takes the lock?
How is the session check synchronized without first taking the session lock in the opposite order or leaving a race between the check and later lock acquisition?
What reserves an admitted request’s right to finish between its session check and its later acquisition of the import/session locks?

quotes:
A sign-out is applied in turn with the session's other requests that
   change it: one admitted before it completes its change to the store, and
   leaves nothing in the ended session.

Validity is
   checked when a request arrives (A04 rule 6, stage 1); a request that
   passes it completes even if a limit or a sign-out comes while it runs, and
   a restart that interrupts it leaves nothing of it (A04 rule 4).
judgement.why: P18 already judged the semantic reservation of an admitted request against sign-out or expiry; the implementation mechanism may vary while preserving that required result.

precedent.topic: Session-validity and locking rules for requests racing sign-out or expiry
quotes:
A sign-out is applied in turn with the session's other requests that
   change it: one admitted before it completes its change to the store, and
   leaves nothing in the ended session.
precedent.why: A request admitted before sign-out completes its store change even if it acquires the session lock later, while no state remains in the ended session.

topics.topic: Secret and backup-key text decoding, byte length, normalization, and comparison
questions: How are environment-variable text values converted to bytes for the 32-byte check, constant-time comparison and distinctness check, including non-ASCII text and any normalization?
Are the 32 bytes the encoded environment text, decoded hexadecimal/base64 material, or some other representation?
What exact key representations and lengths are accepted by the backup encryption scheme?
Which bytes are measured and compared: encoded environment text, decoded hexadecimal/base64 data, or another representation?

quotes:
A secret — each token, the owner credential and the backup key — is at
   least 32 bytes long; a shorter one fails the start.

A presented secret is compared in constant time; no secret enters a record,
   a log line, an audit entry, a diagnostic or an answer (R0-23, R0-37).
judgement.why: P10 already assigns secret decoding, byte measurement, normalization, equality and comparison representation to State 6.

topics.topic: Backup audit-sequence metadata for empty or pruned audit histories
questions: How is the recorded last sequence number defined and checked when the store has never written an audit entry, or when old entries were erased and the durable next-sequence counter is greater than the highest remaining entry?
What value is recorded and what check is performed when the snapshot's audit log is empty?

quotes:
It
   records, readable without its key, its instant, the release that made it,
   the last audit sequence number it holds and a digest of the key it was
   made with (never the key); its age is counted from that instant.

Second, it
   writes the backup under a temporary name and checks it: it decrypts it
   into a second temporary file, opens that for reading only, checks that it
   is the store version of its release, that the store's own integrity check
   passes and that its audit log ends at the recorded sequence number, and
   removes it; a backup that passes is renamed to its kept name, one that
   fails is deleted.
judgement.why: P8 already assigns empty-log sequence representation and its encoded validation rule to State 6.

topics.topic: Startup temporary or probe filename and stale-file cleanup policy
questions: What exact name identifies a probe, when does the next start remove it, and does failure to remove an old probe stop startup or merely produce a diagnostic?

quotes:
A failed start leaves no
   file it made but a probe it could not remove, which the next start or run
   removes with the other temporary files.

When the store's
   configured file does not exist and its directory does, Registry makes a new,
   empty store of the running release's version there at the start, under a

judgement.why: The concrete filename is a later format detail, but the texts do not decide the State 2 refusal behavior when mandatory stale-file cleanup fails.

topics.topic: The event at which the backup snapshot instant is recorded
questions: Is the recorded instant the transaction's snapshot/start time, the end of serialization, or the successful kept-file rename time?
At what event is the backup instant captured for its filename, UTC date, newest-backup display and 30-day retention age?

quotes:
A backup is a consistent copy of the store taken while Registry runs:
   one snapshot of the store, as one read transaction sees it, while other
   transactions go on; it never holds part of a transaction, and its
   recorded instant and last sequence number are those of that snapshot.

A kept
   name is made from the backup's instant and is never overwritten: a backup
   whose kept name exists, or whose rename fails, is deleted and the run
   fails.

The
   owner interface shows the instant of the newest kept backup whose record
   can be read, or that there is none.
judgement.divergence: One implementation records the read transaction's snapshot-acquisition instant, while another records completion or successful rename; the owner sees different newest-backup times, and retention, date assignment and filename-collision behavior can differ.
judgement.why: The phrase 'instant of that snapshot' does not select an event in the multi-stage backup operation.

topics.topic: Whether backup retention remains bounded during delayed or long-running jobs
questions: Is 31 days a hard bound, or can an overlapping, delayed or arbitrarily long run extend retention even when runs do not otherwise fail?
Does the 31-day statement include backup-run duration and skipped runs caused by a still-running successful run, or is it only a scheduling estimate under an additional completion-time assumption?

quotes:
While the daily runs succeed, an erasure reaches the backups by the first
   run after the last backup holding the erased values is 30 days old — at
   most 31 days after the erasure — and a failed or missed run lengthens that
   by the days until a run succeeds.

Registry bounds neither how long a run takes nor how
   old the newest kept backup may be.

Runs
   never overlap: a 03:00 that finds a run still going makes no run of its
   own.
judgement.why: The first passage promises an at-most-31-day result while runs succeed, but the latter passages allow a successful run to take without bound and cause later scheduled runs to be skipped, so successful operation need not meet that bound.

topics.topic: Backup-key rotation and handling backups whose old key is unavailable

topics.topic: Canonical on-disk backup file and record format across releases

topics.topic: Coordination of concurrent Registry startups
questions: What happens if two Registry processes start concurrently against the same store and backup locations, including competing probe files, temporary-store cleanup and final rename?

topics.topic: Digest algorithm and encoding for file identity and confirmation binding
questions: Which digest algorithm and canonical encoding define the file identity and the confirmation binding?

topics.topic: Locking required when an accepted import clears other sessions' uploads
